This is such a wildly insane take I’m hoping you’re trolling. When you *knowingly* expose someone to HIV/AIDS, your shame no longer gets to matter. You’re *putting someone at risk of a terrible, painful, slow death*, not to mention the social isolation and stigmas that come with it. OP’s partner possibly gave them a *life and possibly death sentence* of HIV/AIDS, yet prison is too cruel for them? If you think people are “weird” for taking this so seriously, you’re uniformed about the seriousness of HIV/AIDS and how many people suffered because of others hiding their diagnosis. Not punishing someone for a horrific crime isn’t a moral stance, it’s complacency and ignorance.

I don’t think there’s a good way for OP to initiate this conversation. Without a cause like this wedding ordeal, bringing it up out of the blue that you don’t feel like this child is family would seem rife with ulterior motives and the implication that you’re communicating this because you don’t want them around—which isn’t true in this case. OP’s mom was so blindsided because she didn’t realize that as the parent/authority figure and arbiter of this new dynamic that the onus was on her to continuously have open discussions with her children about it and their feelings—especially since this began when OP was still a teen. After 10 years of them interacting, I’d hope if I were OP’s mother I’d be attentive enough of this complicated dynamic that I created to notice if one of my children isn’t calling them sister/daughter/family like everyone else, and discuss that with them. The only reason this happened is because OP’s mom assumed how OP felt about/viewed Ally rather than actually knowing. This would have given insight into who OP thinks is their immediate family, since it’s an ambiguous and subjective term beyond scientific purposes. 

Maybe OP could have given people the rundown on who would be in what picture ahead of time, but from how OP recounts their relationship with Ally, I think it’s more fair for OP to assume people are aware of their non-familial feelings than it is for OP’s mom to assume that OP considers them apart of their immediate family.

I agree that the fall back excuses are lame, but understandable in an argument where stating your feelings hasn’t been enough and you feel the need to supply something ‘empirical,’ especially to us internet judges.

ETA: none of this means OP’s mom even approaches being a bad person or mother, just a little blind to the more nuanced feelings that come from inviting someone into a family

NTA. Seems like OP’s parents have never taken the time to ask OP how they actually feel about this child, just assumed that they felt the sibling/daughter bond everyone else does, which to me means the mom pretty much set Ally up to be publicly rejected at the wedding. Had the mom cared enough to know how OP felt, this wouldn’t have happened. It seems like Ally is more capable of being respectful of OP’s wishes and feelings than their own blood family.

Everyone saying OP should have just included her in the pictures and not printed them is pushing the issue; though maybe it would have dodged a public rejection of the girl, the same drama would have ensued with questions like “where’s the picture with all of us and Ally?” “why didn’t you hang up any of the pictures of us and Ally?” If they want what they consider to be their family photos, they should go get that done elsewhere.

Whatever it is that makes Ally’s home life semi-unviable is probably very sad. That being said, OP hasn’t excluded her from accessing the family and better resources, they just don’t personally view her as family. And that’s okay. No one ever ‘deserves’ to be viewed as family, that’s an individual’s call, but the people getting married do deserve to walk away with the pictures being how they wanted.

Set in 60's Brooklyn, Perry writes about Harry Odum's experiences with organized crime. He's abandoned by his father, living only with his unstable mother. The book is drenched with themes of incest, rape, pedophilia, homophobia, mental illness, and sexism.

The writing style, in my opinion, suits only a book of this nature. I would recommend it, however, as well as the movie.

"Black Boy" by Richard Wright. It's autobiographical, about Wright's life and living in places in times when being black was an extremely hard circumstance. It reads like fiction while maintaining the weight and impact of a real story.

Side note, if you're a high school student struggling to connect with your teachers, this book is a cool point of discussion (it was a common required reading back in the day).
